title: Creating and altering tables, data types and constraints

videos.script: Two lessons of design, and now you write it down. This one is the statements themselves — CREATE TABLE, the types, and the part nobody teaches, which is how you change a table that already has ten million rows in it. {{statements}} Start with the types, because the mistake here is the one that is cheapest to avoid and most expensive to meet. A column is not a box that holds anything. It is a promise about every value that will ever be in it, and the promise is enforced. {{promise}} Get one wrong and you find out late. Money in a floating-point column adds up wrong by a few cents over a thousand invoices. A timestamp with no timezone is correct on your laptop and an hour out in October. Neither of those errors announces itself. {{late}} Then the second half, which is the one you will actually spend your time on. Creating a table is easy because nothing depends on it yet. Changing one is different: there are rows in it, there are programs reading from it, and some changes take a lock that stops all of them. {{changing}} Which changes are instant, which rewrite the whole table, and what order to do them in so that nothing is down while you do — that is the part that separates somebody who knows SQL from somebody who can be trusted with a database. {{order}}
